title: Toddlers Who Pick Up What You Dropped
text:
At the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, Felix Warneken and Michael Tomasello asked whether helping others is something children must be taught or something that appears on its own.

They invited eighteen-month-old toddlers into a room to play, and then an adult, who had barely interacted with the child, ran into small problems. He was hanging towels with clothespins and dropped one out of reach. He tried to put a stack of books into a cabinet, but his hands were full and the doors were closed. He was searching for a spoon that had fallen through a hole into a box. The adult did not ask for help, did not look at the child at first and did not thank or praise the child afterward.

Most toddlers helped, often within seconds: they picked up the clothespin and handed it over, toddled over to open the cabinet doors, or reached for the spoon. Crucially, in control situations where the adult deliberately threw the clothespin down or did not seem to need anything, the children rarely acted. They were responding to a goal they understood, not just handing things over.

The researchers found that young chimpanzees raised by humans also helped in some simple reaching tasks, suggesting deep evolutionary roots for this behavior.
lesson: Small children are born ready to help. Let them, even when it is slower, and do not drown the impulse in rewards it never needed.
location: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig, Germany
source: Warneken, F., and Tomasello, M. (2006). Altruistic helping in human infants and young chimpanzees. Science, 311(5765), 1301-1303.
